S2.title: Wikipedia EN, History of Pittsburgh
S2.quote: 1760 first houses around Fort Pitt; 1794 courthouse; 1816 city; 1818 first Monongahela bridge; 1841 Second Court House; 10 Apr 1845 Great Fire (over 1,000 buildings); 1854 PRR to Philadelphia; 1857: 939 factories; 1859 coke; 1865 over half the steel and a third of the glass of the U.S.; 1877 railroad riots; 1892 Homestead; 1901 Carnegie sells; 1907 Allegheny City annexed; 1911 half the nation's steel; 1936 flood 46 ft; WWII 95 million tons of steel; 1946 Renaissance I; Lower Hill cleared late 1950s; 1970 U.S. Steel Tower and Three Rivers Stadium; 1974 Point State Park; 1981-82 mills lay off 153,000; 1985 Gulf Oil buyout; 1991 Homestead Works demolished; 2001 Heinz Field and PNC Park

S3.title: Wikipedia EN, Fort Duquesne
S3.quote: Work on Fort Prince George began 17 Feb 1754; by 18 April a French force of five hundred forced the British garrison to surrender; the French knocked down the tiny fort and built Fort Duquesne; destroyed by the French before the British conquest in Nov 1758

S4.title: Wikipedia EN, Fort Pitt (Pennsylvania)
S4.quote: Fort Pitt was built 1759-1761 as a pentagon with bastions by Capt. Harry Gordon; siege from 22 June 1763 relieved at Bushy Run 10 Aug; 1777 Continental Army western headquarters (Gen. Edward Hand)

S5.title: Wikipedia EN, Timeline of Pittsburgh
S5.quote: 1754 Fort Duquesne established by French (April); 9 Jul 1755 British Army defeated; 25 Nov 1758 British take Fort Duquesne; 1764 Fort Pitt Blockhouse completed; 1792 Fort Pitt abandoned; 1794 borough; 1797 Fort Pitt decommissioned and demolished; 18 Mar 1816 city; 1834/35; 1845 Great Fire; 1868 annexations; 1870 Monongahela Incline (28 May); 1872 South Side; 1877 Duquesne Incline; 1883 Smithfield Street Bridge; 1907 Allegheny annexed; 1959 Fort Pitt Bridge (19 Jun); 1960 Fort Pitt Tunnel; 1969 Fort Duquesne Bridge (17 Oct); 1970 Three Rivers Stadium; population 1800 1,565, 1810 4,768, 1820 7,248, 1830 12,542, 1860 49,221, 1900 321,616, 1950 676,806, 1970 540,025, 1980 423,938, 1990 369,879

S6.title: Wikipedia EN, Great Fire of Pittsburgh
S6.quote: 10 April 1845; a third of the city burned, 60 acres, as many as 1,200 buildings, 2,000 families displaced, 2 dead; the Monongahela bridge burned; state grants $50,000 and a three-year tax holiday

S7.title: Wikipedia EN, Pittsburgh flood of 1936
S7.quote: 17-18 March 1936, crest about 46 ft, 21 ft above flood stage; 65 percent of the downtown business district under water from the Point to Grant Street; at least 69 deaths in western Pennsylvania, 45 in the city; 60,000 steelworkers out of work

S8.title: Wikipedia EN, Mellon Arena (Civic Arena)
S8.quote: To make room for the arena about 8,000 residents and 400 businesses were displaced from the lower Hill District; demolition began in 1955 and finished by 1960; opened 17 Sept 1961; demolition began 26 Sept 2011

S9.title: Wikipedia EN, Three Rivers Stadium
S9.quote: Ground broken April 1968; opened 16 July 1970; last game 16 Dec 2000; imploded in 2001

S10.title: Wikipedia EN, Smithfield Street Bridge
S10.quote: Built 1881-1883, opened 19 March 1883 (Lindenthal lenticular truss); a wooden bridge of 1818 was destroyed in the Great Fire of 1845, then a Roebling suspension bridge

S11.title: Wikipedia EN, Point State Park
S11.quote: Land acquired from industrial enterprises in the 1950s; park opened August 1974 with its fountain; outlines of Fort Pitt and Fort Duquesne laid in granite; Manchester and Point bridges removed in 1970

S12.title: Wikipedia EN, Carnegie Steel Company
S12.quote: Formed 1 July 1892; Homestead acquired 1883, open-hearth 1886; sold in 1901 to become part of U.S. Steel

S14.title: Wikipedia EN, Hill District
S14.quote: Cultural center of Black life and a major center of jazz from the years before WWI; in the summer of 1956 some 1,300 structures were razed, displacing about 1,500 families (more than 8,000 residents)

S15.title: Wikipedia EN, Homestead strike
S15.quote: Lockout and strike at the Homestead Steel Works in 1892; battle with Pinkerton agents on 6 July 1892; defeat for the union

S16.title: Wikipedia EN, Great Railroad Strike of 1877
S16.quote: Strikers in Pittsburgh burned 39 buildings, 104 engines and 1,200-1,383 freight cars (S2 says more than 40 buildings, 100 engines, 1,000 cars, 40 men dead)

S17.title: Wikipedia EN, Cathedral of Learning

S18.title: Wikipedia EN, Gulf Tower

S19.title: Wikipedia EN, PPG Place
S19.quote: Groundbreaking 28 January 1981; buildings opened 1983-1984; dedication ceremony 11 April 1984

S20.title: Wikipedia EN, PNC Park

S21.title: Wikipedia EN, Homestead Steel Works
S21.quote: The plant closed in 1986 because of a severe downturn in the domestic steel industry

S22.title: Wikipedia EN, Jones and Laughlin Steel Corporation
S22.quote: First firm to bear the name organized in 1861; steel from 1886; merged with Republic Steel in 1984

zones.name: Pittsburgh village and Golden Triangle (Point to Grant Street)
zones.note: Hand-drawn outline of the Golden Triangle (+-100 m, NOT surveyed). Predecessors of today's downtown buildings are born in a ramp from the Fort Pitt seed (1760: "lower town" houses near the ramparts, S2) to Grant Street by 1850, and die when the current building is built. About 1,200 buildings burned in 1845 (S6): see the fire.

zones.name: Allegheny City (North Side)
zones.note: Town of Allegheny laid out 1788, borough 1828, city 1840, annexed 1907 (S5, S2). Outline and ramp are guesses.

zones.name: Birmingham and the South Side flats
zones.note: South Side became part of the city in 1872 (S5). Birmingham borough start (1811) is general knowledge, not re-read: [Guessing].

zones.name: Hill District
zones.note: The hills east of town were undeveloped in 1845 except the courthouse (S6); a free Black community is documented from the early 19th century (S14). Ramp 1830-1900 is a guess.

zones.name: Strip District and Lawrenceville
zones.note: Lawrenceville was annexed in 1868 (S5). Outline and ramp are guesses.

walls.name: Fort Duquesne (French, 1754-58)
walls.note: Square with corner bastions, 70 m side: schematic. Built from April 1754 (S3); destroyed by the French on 24 Nov 1758, Forbes occupies the ruins on 25 Nov (S3, S11). Position near the tip of the Point (the Fort Pitt site is "near but not directly on" it, S4): +-100 m, to be moved on the granite outlines in Point State Park (OSM). Walls drawn ~8 m thick and 6-7 m high (real palisade/earth ramparts are thinner) so they read from 600-1000 m; bastion towers 16 m wide.

walls.name: Fort Pitt (British, 1759-97)
walls.note: Pentagon with five bastions, Capt. Harry Gordon (S4); built 1759-61 (S4); abandoned 1792, decommissioned and demolished in 1797 (S5; demolition span 1797.6-1798.8 is a guess). Circumradius 95 m and centre are schematic (+-100 m). The Block House (1764) is a separate landmark. Closed line, not "ring", so that it does not become WALL_P (Valencia-specific code in build_render). Walls drawn ~8 m thick and 6-7 m high (real palisade/earth ramparts are thinner) so they read from 600-1000 m; bastion towers 16 m wide.

gutting.name: Lower Hill District (cleared 1955-60)
gutting.note: About 1,300 structures razed in the summer of 1956 (S14); demolition 1955-60 (S8). Today this land is the arena lawn and parking, so no current building exists to hang a predecessor on: the kit fills the empty part of this ring with row-house lots from the Hill zone ramp, and removes them 1955.5-1956.8. Ring is ~35 ha (the clearance was 95 acres = 38 ha, S2). The last building, Bethel AME Church (1960), is not modelled.

gutting.name: Point warehouses and rail yards (cleared 1950-53)
gutting.note: The Point was industrial until the 1950s: land taken from industrial enterprises for the park (S11); vast swaths near the Point demolished for Gateway Center by 1950 (S2). From 1800, after Fort Pitt is gone (1797), lots fill the void of the park; they go in 1952-53. Hand-drawn 36-acre outline.

fires.name: Great Fire of 1845
fires.note: Started 10 April 1845 (=1845.268) near Ferry Street and burned about 60 acres, as many as 1,200 buildings (S6). The real fire lasted hours; the window 1845.268-1845.30 (12 days) is only so that flames are visible during a 6 s hover. Ring is a ~27 ha sketch of the burned south-west of downtown ending at Market Square (+-100 m, NOT surveyed). destroy acts only on predecessor buildings from the zones (today's downtown is 1900+).

floods.name: 1936 St. Patrick's Day flood (1)
floods.note: Rings from fetch_pgh.py flood 46: DEM cells below 224.94 m (738 ft = gauge zero 692 ft + 46 ft) connected to the rivers; normal pool 710 ft. depth is the kit's constant draped depth (test value). 1936 flood: kept as an ordinary event (card), NOT a stop: the draped-water visual is a known limitation.

landmarks.note: Opened 28 May 1870 (=1870.4), S5; "built 1870 by John Endres" (S13). Coordinates Wikipedia vs OSM 51 m apart. Only the lower station is modelled; no track.

landmarks.name: Carnegie Museum and Library (Oakland)
landmarks.note: First gallery 5 Nov 1895 (=1895.85); Carnegie founded the Carnegie Institute in 1895 (S2). The Forbes Avenue building was 1907 (Wikipedia text): which footprint the kit picks is unchecked. Start 1893.5 is a guess.

landmarks.name: Forbes Field
landmarks.note: Opened 30 June 1909 (=1909.49), Timeline S5; verified by 2 sources (S13). Fire 17 July 1971, demolition began 11 days later = 28 July 1971 (=1971.57), S32; the end of the demolition (1971.95) is a guess. Wikipedia vs Wikidata coordinates differ ~150 m. landmarks.name: Cathedral of Learning

landmarks.name: Wabash Pittsburgh Terminal
landmarks.note: Opened 13 April 1904 (=1904.28), closed 31 Oct 1931, demolished Oct 1953 - early 1954 (Wikipedia, S13); 197 ft = 60 m. No footprint in the data (demolished): default 65 x 45 m block with a dome, schematic.

landmarks.name: Civic Arena
landmarks.note: Opened 17 Sept 1961 (=1961.71), verified by 2 sources (S8, S13); under construction in 1957 (S8), a steel strike halted work in July 1959 (S8). Demolition began 26 Sept 2011 (S8); the end (31 Mar 2012) is from Wikidata/Wikipedia list (S13), not rechecked. Round plan 126 m (S8: roof diameter 415 ft), schematic dome.

landmarks.name: Three Rivers Stadium

landmarks.name: U.S. Steel Tower
landmarks.note: 256.3 m, 64 floors; dedication 30 Sept 1971 (S28); CONFLICT: the tallest list and infobox give completion 1970, Wikidata 1971. The model is complete from 1970.9; start 1967.5 is [Guessing]. Triangular plan comes from the footprint (auto).

open: Buildings placed in their documented years.
title: PITTSBURGH
1754 TO NOW

cards.title: The Forks of the Ohio
lines: Virginians begin Fort Prince George at the Forks of the Ohio in February 1754.
About 500 French soldiers force them out in April and build Fort Duquesne.
They keep the Forks for four years and beat a British army in 1755.

cards.title: Pittsburgh gets its name
lines: The French blow up Fort Duquesne on November 24, 1758. General Forbes names the ruins for William Pitt.
The British build Fort Pitt in 1759-61 and hold it through the siege of 1763.

cards.title: The Block House
lines: Colonel Bouquet adds a brick redoubt in 1764.
It still stands: the oldest authenticated building west of the Alleghenies.

cards.title: Headquarters of the West
lines: In 1777 Fort Pitt becomes a U.S. fort under Gen. Edward Hand.
It serves as the American headquarters of the western war.

cards.title: A borough on the frontier
lines: Pittsburgh is incorporated as a borough in 1794.
That summer farmers angry about the whiskey tax march on the town.

cards.title: Fort Pitt is torn down
lines: The army abandoned the fort in 1792 and decommissioned it in 1797, and it was demolished.
In the same year Pittsburgh begins making glass.
cards.note: Timeline S5: 1792 abandoned, 3 Aug 1797 decommissioned and "subsequently demolished"; demolition date itself not found.

cards.title: The first steamboat
lines: The first steamboat is built in Pittsburgh in 1811.
By 1800 the town had 1,565 people and over 60 shops.

cards.title: A city at last
lines: Pittsburgh is incorporated as a city on March 18, 1816.
The War of 1812 had cut off British goods and turned it into a factory town.

cards.title: The first bridge
lines: A wooden bridge across the Monongahela opens in 1818, where the Smithfield Street Bridge stands today.
It will burn in the fire of 1845.

cards.title: Canal and locomotive
lines: The Main Line Canal to Philadelphia is completed in 1834.
In 1835 a Pittsburgh firm builds the first locomotive west of the Alleghenies.

cards.title: A courthouse on Grant's Hill
lines: The second Allegheny County courthouse, of gray sandstone, is finished in 1841.
The hill around it is still open ground.

cards.title: The city rebuilds
lines: Pennsylvania grants $50,000 and a three-year tax holiday after the fire.
The demand for new homes and goods drives the iron and glass works.

cards.title: The railroads arrive
lines: The Ohio and Pennsylvania Railroad reaches Allegheny City in 1851.
The Pennsylvania Railroad links Pittsburgh to Philadelphia in 1854.
cards.note: Timeline S5 dates the Pennsylvania Railroad service to 1852; S2 says 1854 for Philadelphia service.

cards.title: 939 factories
lines: An 1857 count lists 939 factories in Pittsburgh and Allegheny City.
In steam tonnage it is the nation's third busiest port.

cards.title: Coke and steel
lines: In 1859 the Clinton and Soho furnaces introduce coke smelting.
Pittsburgh begins the move from iron to steel.

cards.title: Arsenal of the Union
lines: By the end of the Civil War Pittsburgh makes over half of the nation's steel.
It also makes more than a third of its glass.

cards.title: The city swallows its neighbors
lines: In 1868 Pittsburgh annexes Lawrenceville and the townships of Pitt, Oakland and others to the east.
The South Side joins in 1872.

cards.title: Bessemer steel at Braddock
lines: In 1875 Carnegie's Edgar Thomson Works begins making steel rails with the Bessemer process.
The mill lies upriver, beyond the edge of this map.

cards.title: A second incline
lines: The Duquesne Incline opens on May 20, 1877, seven years after the Monongahela Incline.
Both lift workers up Mount Washington.

cards.title: The railroad strike
lines: In July 1877 strikers burn about 40 buildings, 100 locomotives and over 1,000 rail cars.
Forty men die; Pittsburgh is the most violent city of the national strike.
cards.note: Counts differ: S2 more than 40 buildings, 100 engines, 1,000 cars, 40 dead; S16 39 buildings, 104 engines, 1,200-1,383 freight cars.

cards.title: Electricity and open-hearth steel
lines: George Westinghouse founds Westinghouse Electric in 1886.
The same year Carnegie installs open-hearth furnaces at Homestead.

cards.title: Homestead
lines: Carnegie Steel is formed on July 1, 1892. Five days later strikers and Pinkertons fight at Homestead.
Ten men die and the union loses. The mill lies just beyond this map.

cards.title: Steel pays for a museum
lines: The Carnegie Institute opens in Oakland in 1895; the first gallery opens on November 5.
Library, museums and music hall are financed by Andrew Carnegie.

cards.title: U.S. Steel
lines: In 1901 Carnegie sells his mills to J.P. Morgan for $250 million.
They become part of the new U.S. Steel.

cards.title: The Frick Building
lines: Henry Clay Frick's office tower is finished in March 1902.
It is one of the first downtown skyscrapers.

cards.title: Union Station
lines: The Pennsylvania Railroad opens Union Station in 1903.
Its rotunda still stands.

cards.title: Allegheny City joins Pittsburgh
lines: In 1907 Pittsburgh annexes Allegheny City, today the North Side.

cards.title: Forbes Field
lines: Forbes Field opens in Oakland on June 30, 1909.
The Pirates win their first World Series that October.

cards.title: Half of America's steel
lines: By 1911 Pittsburgh is producing half of the nation's steel.
Smoke is a sign of prosperity.

cards.title: The Strip
lines: By the 1920s the Strip District, from 11th to 33rd Street, is the city's economic center: wholesalers, produce dealers, auction houses.
Before them came mills and the Fort Pitt Foundry.
cards.note: S33 gives no single year; 1923 is thematic ("by the 1920s").

cards.title: Three Sisters
lines: Three matching bridges cross the Allegheny between 1926 and 1928.
Seventh Street opens in June 1926, Ninth in November 1926 and Sixth in September 1928.

cards.title: The Gulf Tower
lines: The Gulf Tower is finished in 1932 with a stepped pyramid on top.
It is the tallest building in Pittsburgh until 1970.

cards.title: The St. Patrick's Day flood
lines: On March 18, 1936 the rivers crest at 46 feet, 21 feet over flood stage. Downtown is under water from the Point to Grant Street.
At least 69 people die in western Pennsylvania and 60,000 steelworkers lose their jobs.

cards.title: The Cathedral of Learning
lines: The 42-story Cathedral of Learning is formally dedicated in June 1937; its exterior was finished in 1934.

cards.title: Arsenal of Democracy
lines: In World War II Pittsburgh's mills deliver 95 million tons of steel.
The city fills with workers from the South.

cards.title: Smoke and a new plan
lines: Mayor David Lawrence enforces the Smoke Control Ordinance from 1946.
The first Renaissance begins.

cards.title: The old Point comes down
lines: Gateway Center replaces the warehouses and rail yards near the Point from 1950.
The Wabash Terminal, open since 1904, is demolished in 1953-54.
cards.note: Gateway Center start: S2 says vast swaths near the Point were demolished by 1950; Wabash terminal dates from Wikipedia (S13).

cards.title: The Lower Hill is cleared
lines: In 1956 about 1,300 structures are razed and more than 8,000 people lose their homes.
Most are Black; the district was a center of jazz. The work runs from 1955 to 1960.
cards.note: S14: 1,300 structures, about 1,500 families, more than 8,000 residents, summer 1956; S8: 8,000 residents and 400 businesses, demolition 1955-60; S2: 95 acres.

cards.title: The Fort Pitt Bridge
lines: The Fort Pitt Bridge opens on June 19, 1959; the Fort Pitt Tunnel follows in 1960.
The Point becomes the gateway for cars.

cards.title: The Bridge to Nowhere
lines: The Fort Duquesne Bridge opens on October 17, 1969.
Parts of it had stood for years without a connection.
cards.note: S13: built 1958-63 but not connected, opened 17 Oct 1969.

cards.title: Three Rivers Stadium
lines: Three Rivers Stadium opens on the North Shore on July 16, 1970.
The Pirates and Steelers play there until 2000.

cards.title: The U.S. Steel Tower
lines: The U.S. Steel Tower is dedicated on September 30, 1971.
At 256 meters it is the tallest building in Pittsburgh.

cards.title: Point State Park
lines: The park opens in August 1974 with its fountain at the tip of the Golden Triangle.
Granite lines mark the outlines of Fort Pitt and Fort Duquesne.

cards.title: The mills close
lines: After the 1981-82 recession the steel mills lay off 153,000 workers.
Closures ripple through railroads, mines and factories.

cards.title: A headquarters town loses its headquarters
lines: In 1985 Gulf Oil is bought in what was then the largest buyout in history.
More than 1,000 white-collar jobs vanish in one day.

cards.title: The mills come down
lines: The Homestead Works closes in 1986 and is demolished in 1991.
In the 1990s the Homestead, Duquesne and South Side J&L sites are cleared. The mills are not in this model.
cards.note: Honest limit: the mills are demolished and absent from the footprint data.

cards.title: Medicine replaces steel
lines: Medicine has replaced steel as a leading industry.
Tourism booms: nearly 3,000 hotel rooms open after 2004.
cards.note: Year is thematic: S2 says "since 2004"; no single date.

cards.title: A new arena across the street
lines: The Penguins move to a new arena in 2010.
The Civic Arena, the first major arena with a retractable roof, closes.

cards.title: The Igloo comes down
lines: Demolition of the Civic Arena begins on September 26, 2011.
The cleared Lower Hill site waits for new buildings.

cards.title: The newest tower
lines: The FNB Financial Center, finished in 2024, is the newest tower on the skyline.
cards.note: Year from the Wikipedia tallest list (S13); not cross-checked.
